articles.summary: Humans have trouble with inhuman distances. Miles are about the largest comprehensible unit of measurement we have, because we can understand miles. Watering hole is in a mile? No problem, we’ll be there soon. Aurochs herd is 30 miles away? OK, our hunting party won't walk that in a day, but it’s doable. Miles are a good measure for us, and on the scale of the universe, absolutely useless. The Sun is about 93 million miles from Earth. Can that possibly be spatially encompassed by a human mind that evolved to think in terms of footsteps? The nearest star after that is about 25 trillion miles away. We have the words, but they blur into a meaningless litany of zeroes and -illions. How big is the observable universe? 546,710,000,000,000,000,000,000 miles across, best we can tell. What does that mean to us? Nothing. I submit that while it’s less accurate, it’s more truthful to say simply that the universe is “very big.” Enter light. The big picture: Democrats scored overwhelming gains in the midterms after making health care affordability a major priority for the next Congress. articles.summary: It took over a decade to make Grand Theft Auto VI. And when it's released on November 19, it will have already set at least one record: the most expensive video game ever made. In the years since the last GTA release, the video game industry has changed massively. Investors, once excited by the prospect of blockbuster video games, have pulled back, sales have stagnated, and the industry as a whole seems more precarious. Bloomberg News video game reporter Jason Schreier has been following Rockstar Games and its quest to release GTA VI for a long time. Ahead of the launch, we speak with him about why it took 13 years — and a budget that reportedly exceeded $1 billion — to get GTA VI across the finish line, and his impressions of the game having played it before almost anyone else on the planet.
